items.question: Why did you focus on building a map of scent at Google Brain?
items.object: A digital map of scent
items.answer: There's three kind of broad steps. You got to read the world. So, like turn atoms into bits and information. You have to map it, like understand it. So, you know, be able to manipulate it digitally, encode it, send it, and that's like JPEG and RGB, right? And then you have to be able to write it back out again, right? So, a printer or a display or a speaker. And so the thing we focused on at Google Brain was the missing piece, which is for scent is the map. So, color has had a map.

items.object: Maps for representing sound and color
items.answer: So like let's approach it from the side: how did this work for vision? How did this work for hearing? We've had maps for a long time, right? So the map for sound is just one dimension. But of course I'm simplifying a lot because for each of those other modalities, there's lots of different maps.

items.question: How do you think about the physical connection that smelling gives you to another living thing?
items.object: Smell as physical contact between the brain and the living world
items.answer: The equivalent for smell are those cells called olfactory sensory neurons. And those cells actually start in the brain and they poke through your skull and they actually touch the world. It's one of the two parts of your brain that actually leaves the skull. And so when I smell something, my brain is physically touching another living thing that's let off a little bit of some of itself for me to smell. So there are millions and millions of olfactory sensory neurons in the part of your nose, the inside that actually does the smelling, called the olfactory epithelium.
quotes: So, the equivalent for smell are those cells are called olfactory sensory neurons. And so when you smell something, your brain is physically touching another living thing that's let off a little bit of some of itself for you to smell. So there are millions and millions of olfactory sensory neurons in the part of your nose, the inside that actually does the smelling, called the olfactory epithelium.

The response characterizes smelling another living thing as the brain physically touching material released by that organism.

items.question: How do you assess the capabilities of the human sense of smell?
items.object: Human olfactory sensitivity
items.answer: I don't think we have a good estimate for how many smells a person can smell. There is a very famous paper which has a trillion, which has been pretty thoroughly debunked. But I don't know if we can really estimate that. There's a few things, though, when you talk about sensitivity. I had laser eye surgery, so I had glasses for most of my life. I couldn't really see that well. So I couldn't resolve really subtle differences, but I wasn't blind. I could perceive all the light. Light was getting in, but it just wasn't being focused properly. So with smell, as long as your airways are working, you can smell and detect things. You might not detect subtle differences, but you definitely are sensitive to it. And some people aren't, and they have their airways closed for various reasons, like anatomical or an injury or something like that. But there's this amazing experiment by Noam Sobel, who showed that actually people can do scent tracking. If you put on a blindfold and you get somebody down on the ground and you leave a little trail of chocolate or cinnamon or whatever, people, if they concentrate, can actually scent track just like a dog. They're super slow, but they can do it. So that just goes to show that there's this myth that we're not good at smelling. We're freaking amazing at smelling. We can smell the equivalent for some molecules of one little teardrop in an Olympic-size swimming pool. We are so sensitive to some things. I mean, that's how natural gas has a smell. It's just the tiniest amount of these molecules called mercaptan are added to it and we can smell it super sensitively, like parts per billion or trillion. It's crazy. So, I mean, we're good. Humans are good at smelling.

items.question: How did you establish that your neural network's predictions of odor from molecular structure were human quality?
items.object: Predicting odor from molecular structure and the odor Turing test
items.answer: Step number one for us was there's a really basic version of this problem, which is I assume you're only smelling one molecule and you know its structure. You can draw it on the board like you're in high school chemistry class with atoms and bonds and all that, and you know what it smells like. So this particular set of combinations of carbon and nitrogen and oxygen smells like sweet, smells like vanilla, smells like phenolic, smells like chocolate. Those are maybe four descriptors drawn from a set of a hundred that apply to that molecule. Well, okay, go get thousands of those pairs and then train a neural network to predict that relationship from structure to odor. That problem, called the structure odor relation problem, had been unsolved for a hundred years and actually in some cases people thought it was unsolvable. And so what we did as one of our first outputs at Google Brain was we just trained a relatively new at the time kind of neural network called a graph neural network, which was specialized for chemistry. It's actually very related to the transformer. It's kind of been subsumed by the transformer in the intervening years. And we were able to predict what things smell like very well. In fact, so well that we said why don't we set up an odor Turing test. Let's go find molecules that nobody's ever smelled before. Some have never been made before, like nature has not seen them. Let's predict what they smell like ahead of time and keep our predictions secret. Let's go get those molecules physically, send them to another location. I have a great collaborator that I worked with on this. His name is Joel Mainland at Monell. Let's train people to smell and describe smell. It doesn't take a ton of training, maybe like eight hours to do okay at, hey, this smells grassy or phenolic or vanilla or cucumber, and maybe 50 terms you can be trained on. Let's double blind these people to smell and describe completely new molecules and then compare how well this panel of people does to first of all some individual panelist, because one person is always worse than the average of the panel. So let's compare that to our model. The question is basically, the odor Turing test is if you want to make your panel better, would you rather add another person or would you rather add the predictions of a model? And it turned out our model predictions were better than any one individual panelist on average in the panel, meaning we've passed an odor Turing test. Our model predictions were human quality, which was pretty cool.

items.question: Why did you see your neural network's embedding as a promising map of smell?
items.object: The principal odor map
items.answer: What we did with the neural network is we cracked it open and we looked at what's called the embedding layer, which is a part of the neural network that basically turns the inputs into a vector that is the map, and then that map is what we kind of can slice up in regions and use for classification. So this region of the map is vanilla, this region of the map is redberry, etc. Without that you actually can't do that classification problem. So that embedding turned out, if you do the engineering right, it just kind of needs to be around 300 dimensions to work really well, which is suspicious but suggestive. I can't make any claims, but that embedding had a ton of beautiful structure in it and that seemed to be a first candidate for a continuous predictive map of smell and we called it the principal odor map and that's been foundational to what we've built at the company since then.

items.question: Why do you see creating new fragrance molecules with your odor models as an interesting business?
items.object: Developing new fragrance molecules using odor models
items.answer: Actually that was our first line of business that we started: can we somehow make new molecules that smell great and that are safe and that we can produce at scale and that are affordable, all that. And turns out like that's a very interesting business to be in because if you can make some molecules smell great but they're not safe or they're being removed because of new regulatory action, we need replacements because we want our products to smell great, like our laundry to smell great, our home to smell great. And so we actually use these models which we've developed over many years to actually find new fragrance molecules that have never existed in nature before and then we make them and we could bring them to market, which we're in the process of doing right now.

items.question: How do you define the space of molecules that could potentially have a smell?
items.object: Defining the space of physically realizable molecules that could have a smell
items.answer: Yeah. So, we've enumerated all the molecules that could possibly be made. So, as in they're real, actually realizable physical molecules that could possibly have a smell. And we've basically run predictive models on all of them and we've made a huge number of them. So the initial part of that statement is like there's some physics that governs the ways that molecules can form, and we can filter that based on some set of criteria: three atoms to 20 atoms, and maybe these bonds work, these bonds don't work. And then we get some starting place, this list of potential, and there's a manufacturability filter as well.

items.question: How do you think about the architecture behind olfactory intelligence?
items.object: Olfactory intelligence as a coordinated fleet of predictive models
items.answer: So when we say olfactory intelligence, we kind of mean the suite or the fleet of predictive models on all aspects of smell, and there's dozens of models. If you go look at Neolabs or life sciences companies, some of them are pretty upfront that their core model or foundation model is actually a fleet of models, and that's how self-driving cars work too. Self-driving cars are driven by a fleet of models that all connect together along a spine to coordinate sensing with action with planning and all that stuff. So we're, I think, close—the way we think about it is closer to autonomous vehicles, which is actually where my CTO's background is.

items.question: How do you understand what makes a scent smell good to a particular consumer?
items.object: Consumer preferences for scents and flavors
items.answer: It's a derived property of the scent, coupled with the target consumer. So, you know, an example is like you could either choose parmesan cheese or kimchi or strawberry. Depending on who you show it to, they may or may not like it. And in the case of strawberry, actually the kind of strawberries that people think of or want in Japan are pretty different from the ones that we think of or want in the US. Just the flavor of them, it's a different sweetness profile. It's almost borderline different fruit in terms of how you construct it in a product. But what you like is heavily driven by what you've been exposed to before and what did you feel like when you got exposed to it? And, you know, if you're in a Korean household, being exposed to kimchi is like you do that under warm family conditions. And if you're exposed to kimchi, it could be literally whatever. If you're a non-Korean person who's never experienced it before, you're like, "What did I just open?" I happen to love kimchi, but it was an acquired taste. items.question: How do you understand the relative contributions of smell and taste to flavor?
items.object: The relationship between smell, taste, and flavor
items.answer: So there's kind of three aspects to this. So there's smell, which is for sure just what comes in your nose but also you can smell things that go the other way. It's called retronasal action. So when you're eating something you're actually creating this chimney effect that kind of has scent vent the reverse way. And so this is how flavor is produced. If you ever eat a jelly bean and hold your nose, it just tastes sweet. You can't tell if it's lemon or lime or grapefruit or whatever. So flavor is 90% smell, 10% taste. And taste is just what happens on your tongue, like sweet, savory, sour, salty, umami, all that, and bitter. But in terms of dimensionality and richness—again, I'm sure the taste neuroscientists would kill me for saying this—but it's just not as complex.

items.question: How do you think about the path toward giving computers a sense of smell?
items.object: Building computers with a sense of smell
items.answer: Like I want to give computers a sense of smell and that means reading and mapping and writing smell. And we've been on our journey super pragmatic about building the scientific capabilities, which is the first two years of the company, and then finding a great business to put this to use in, which is the fragrance industry. But we're going to go further than that. In fact, we're talking with a number of organizations. I think the thing that's needed now for not just design of scent, but the detection of scent, is exactly what you're talking about from before, which is we have to build a foundation model. And the thing that's been missing and that we've been building is you have to collect a whole bunch of data. items.question: How do you think about the work of collecting new data to expand what AI can do?
items.object: Collecting new data to expand AI's capabilities
items.answer: A whole lot harder than scraping Reddit. But it's worth it because literally nobody's going to do it unless we pull ourselves together. But this is worth doing. As an aside, I have a lot of friends in the world of AI and ML and I came in through this as a biologist and as a biologist you go do experiments and it's hard and you got to go to the bench and get your own data and it's gritty. And in the world of AI you kind of just assume the data is out there and if the data is not out there you kind of assume you can give somebody a credit card to create the data. And I think that's amazing. But the amount of infrastructure that you have access to is astoundingly huge. And you just have to understand that if you want to continue to expand the realm of what AI can do and compute can do, it might get hard. You might reach a point where there's not a vendor that can handle everything for you and shine your shoes or whatever. You might have to go do the work yourself. And so we're very much in that regime.

items.question: How do you envision building smell into foundation models?
items.object: Foundation models incorporating smell and taste
items.answer: I think where we're going is we are collecting huge amounts of data, but importantly we have this platform that allows us to store all this data, organize it, massive efficiencies of scale digitally and then increasingly physically. We can make a huge number of unique scents. We have all this infrastructure that we've built painstakingly over a few years and now let's go get all the smell data and let's build this chemical slice of reality into AI. Let's build a true foundation model. But the data comes first, right? We need to go get all the data and then whenever these models come out, like Opus 47 or when Mythos comes out or Codex 55, they talk about the model card in terms of all these benchmarks. And so what I imagine for the future is that we'll collect all this foundational data and malaria detection will be a benchmark, and cancer detection will be a benchmark, and building a great market product for a new shampoo launch in Malaysia will be a benchmark.
